name: Playoff Tournament
description: $$$2^k$$$ teams participate in a playoff tournament. The tournament consists of $$$2^k - 1$$$ games. They are held as follows: first of all, the teams are split into pairs: team $$$1$$$ plays against team $$$2$$$, team $$$3$$$ plays against team $$$4$$$ (exactly in this order), and so on (so, $$$2^{k-1}$$$ games are played in that phase). When a team loses a game, it is eliminated, and each game results in elimination of one team (there are no ties). After that, only $$$2^{k-1}$$$ teams remain. If only one team remains, it is declared the champion; otherwise, $$$2^{k-2}$$$ games are played: in the first one of them, the winner of the game "$$$1$$$ vs $$$2$$$" plays against the winner of the game "$$$3$$$ vs $$$4$$$", then the winner of the game "$$$5$$$ vs $$$6$$$" plays against the winner of the game "$$$7$$$ vs $$$8$$$", and so on. This process repeats until only one team remains. For example, this picture describes the chronological order of games with $$$k = 3$$$: Let the string $$$s$$$ consisting of $$$2^k - 1$$$ characters describe the results of the games in chronological order as follows: if $$$s_i$$$ is 0 , then the team with lower index wins the $$$i$$$-th game; if $$$s_i$$$ is 1 , then the team with greater index wins the $$$i$$$-th game; if $$$s_i$$$ is ? , then the result of the $$$i$$$-th game is unknown (any team could win this game). Let $$$f(s)$$$ be the number of possible winners of the tournament described by the string $$$s$$$. A team $$$i$$$ is a possible winner of the tournament if it is possible to replace every ? with either 1 or 0 in such a way that team $$$i$$$ is the champion. You are given the initial state of the string $$$s$$$. You have to process $$$q$$$ queries of the following form: $$$p$$$ $$$c$$$ — replace $$$s_p$$$ with character $$$c$$$, and print $$$f(s)$$$ as the result of the query.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le 18$$$). The second line contains a string consisting of $$$2^k - 1$$$ characters — the initial state of the string $$$s$$$. Each character is either ? , 0 , or 1 . The third line contains one integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of queries. Then $$$q$$$ lines follow, the $$$i$$$-th line contains an integer $$$p$$$ and a character $$$c$$$ ($$$1 \le p \le 2^k - 1$$$; $$$c$$$ is either ? , 0 , or 1 ), describing the $$$i$$$-th query.
output_specification: For each query, print one integer — $$$f(s)$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1535D — Playoff Tournament [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
